Good afternoon and happy Friday, everybody. Amina Mohamed, the Deputy Secretary-General, spoke to the Security Council members this morning at an ARIA formula meeting on education in Sudan. She said that among everything the war in Sudan has taken, One of the most significant is the future of Sudan depriving the education of its children. Today, she said, at least 8 million school-aged children remain out of school, with a disproportionate impact on millions of displaced children, especially those seeking refuge outside of Sudan. Since 2024, the United Nations has verified more than 67 attacks on schools across Sudan, while over 154 instances of military use of schools have been reported. The Deputy Secretary-General said that this year, the UN and its partners have brought more than a million Sudanese children back into some form of learning, but it is simply not enough. She said it is time to stop this war and to pull Sudan back from the brink of losing another generation of its children. From the Democratic Republic of the Congo, our colleagues at the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs tell us that children and women continue to bear a disproportionate share of the Ebola outbreak in the eastern province of Ituri. The outbreak is unfolding in a province where nearly one million people are displaced, around 80 percent of them women and children. According to the UN Children's Fund, more than 300 children have died from Ebola since the outbreak began. Children make up nearly a quarter of confirmed cases, but almost a third of all deaths. As we mentioned earlier this week, the outbreak is also severely disrupting essential healthcare. In the hardest hit areas, use of health services has dropped by more than 40% in recent months, as fear of infection keeps people away. The UN Population Fund warns that this fear, combined with overstretched health services, is preventing many pregnant women from seeking care. Maternal deaths in Nturi have nearly doubled since the outbreak began. with about six women dying each week from childbirth-related complications. Ebola infection during pregnancy remains associated with almost universal fetal loss. OCHA stresses that restoring community confidence is key. Together with the Ministry of Public Health, the World Health Organization, and the Africa CDC, UNICEF and partners have deployed 13,000 community workers, reaching more than 2.4 million people with information on Ebola prevention and early detection. They've also carried out over 500,000 household visits to counter misinformation and encourage early care seeking. Meanwhile, WHO reports that its technical advisory group on vaccine research is recommending a clinical trial in the DRC for their VABO vaccine, the only licensed vaccine against Ebola. WHO is working with partners to begin the trial as soon as possible. This comes as the virus continues to spread rapidly across eastern DRC, with total cases now surpassing 4,000 and 1,850 deaths reported. And from South Sudan, OCHA tells us that we and our partners continue to support government-led preparedness efforts against Ebola. While no cases have been confirmed in the country, the outbreak in neighboring Democratic Republic of the Congo, coupled with people moving between borders, continues to pose a risk. These preparedness efforts include surveillance to detect cases early, screening at points of entry, training health workers, providing medical supplies, and community awareness campaigns. This month alone, our health partners screened more than 135,300 travelers at points of entry into South Sudan. More than 300 health workers and frontline personnel have been trained in screening, triage, infection prevention and control, referrals, and safe burials. Over seven tons of emergency supplies have also been pre-positioned in Yambio, near the border with the DRC. But insecurity continues to hamper this work. Between January and July, 451 incidents that blocked or threatened humanitarian operations were reported across South Sudan. Along the Yei-Morobo corridor, 32 humanitarian staff abductions have been recorded since January of last year. Underscoring the challenges of operating the areas at highest risk of Ebola, also in South Sudan, the government and our partners have finalized the 2026 flood. and drought preparedness and response plan. Last year's floods affected more than 1.3 million people, while this year's forecast points to a heightened risk of drought alongside continued flooding in some areas. The plan estimates that floods could affect more than 830,000 people this year, more than a quarter of whom are already displaced, while nearly 1.7 million people could be affected by drought. The plan also includes a $215 million government-led resilience package to strengthen flood infrastructure, early warning systems, and anticipatory action through 2027. The UN Interim Force in Lebanon says there's been a significant reduction in kinetic activity in southern Lebanon today, following two days of intensified Israel Defense Force fire. Yesterday, peacekeepers recorded 129 projectiles, the highest daily figure since the 21st of June, all fired by the IDF. Much of this fire focused on Al Mansouri and nearby areas following the 5th of August incident in which two IDF soldiers were reportedly killed and several others injured. Overnight and until 0900 local time today, UNIFIL recorded 44 IDF projectiles with no further projectiles recorded between 0900 and 1600 hours. UNIFIL also recorded 42 Israeli violations of Lebanese airspace today, with a cumulative overflight time exceeding 127 hours. By 1600 today, peacekeepers had recorded a further 26 airspace violations. UNIFIL patrol discovered two improvised devices along a road near Chakra in Sector East yesterday. UNIFIL explosive ordnance disposal experts destroyed the devices, allowing operations in the area to resume. At sea, peacekeepers positioned in Al Nakoura in Sector West observed two IDF boats crossing into Lebanese waters. One boat deployed two unidentified rectangular objects into the sea before returning to Israeli waters. The second boat remained in nearby Lebanese waters. Turning to the occupied Palestinian territory, the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs reports limited improvements in the flow of critical supplies into Gaza, even as needs remain immense and people continue to depend heavily on aid. Data collected through the UN 2720 mechanism indicate a 33% increase in the volume of supplies that we and our partners were able to bring into Gaza in July compared with June. There's more than 55,000 pallets of aid, roughly 35,000 metric tons or 26,000 truckloads, bringing us closer to the levels recorded before the regional escalation began at the end of February. About 60% of these supplies were food, followed by smaller volumes of shelter, water, sanitation, hygiene and health items. Additional supplies were brought in by the private sector. Still, our humanitarian partners warn that restrictions remain on the types of supplies allowed into Gaza. Specifically, they say more approvals are needed to bring engine oil and spare parts into the Strip because all humanitarian operations depend on vehicles and backup generators that need to be maintained. Repeated denials of requests to bring in engine oil combined with insufficient quantities of quality lubricant oil coming in through the private sector mean that critical operations at hospitals, pumping stations, and bakeries could be reduced or forced to stop. Another restriction is on durable shelter materials. Most of Gaza's 2.1 million people remain displaced in poor conditions, and so far, our humanitarian partners have mostly been allowed to bring in tents that do not last long. To put this in context, a new assessment by the UN satellite center estimates that the number of destroyed structures across Gaza has increased by 9% since the declaration of a ceasefire in October 2025. Overall, about 82% of the structures in Gaza are damaged. That's more than 200,000 structures that are damaged to some degree, and two-thirds of them are assessed to have been destroyed. Turning to the West Bank, today our partners from across the humanitarian community visited Qalandia Camp in Jerusalem to jointly assess people's needs after Israeli forces concluded a two-day operation there. Our teams identified widespread damage to houses and businesses, and dozens of families reported damage to doors, windows, and furniture after Israeli forces spent time inside their homes. Many reported significant financial losses. Forces had reportedly taken over some of the homes, pushed families out, and used those properties as interrogation centers. Our partners with the Palestine Red Crescent Society say that more than 50 people were injured during the two-day operation. And the UN and our partners are mobilizing support for those affected. From Ukraine, our humanitarian colleagues at the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs tell us that attacks between Thursday and this morning have killed and injured several civilians and have also damaged homes and critical civilian infrastructure. The Dnipro region was the hardest hit, And the Kharkiv region, Donetsk, Kherson, Odesa, Sumy, and Zaporizhia were also impacted. OCHA remains alarmed by the impact of the-- Could someone please turn that off? I think it is you, Evelyn. OCHA remains alarmed by the impact of the hostilities on humanitarian operations. Yesterday, Save the Children said that a guided aerial bomb damaged its office in the city of Sumy, marking the second attack on the organization's facilities in Ukraine in less than a week. Our humanitarian colleagues also said that on Wednesday, two staff members of a local NGO that partners with the International Organization for Migration were injured in a drone attack in Kherson. Despite the growing risk to aid operations across Ukraine, we, along with our humanitarian partners, continue to do whatever we can to provide emergency assistance to people impacted by intensified attacks. An update to share from our peacekeeping colleagues, the Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations, Jean-Pierre Lacroix, concluded a seven-day trip yesterday to Fiji and Australia. He was accompanied by Acting Military Adviser Lieutenant General Cheryl Pearce and Police Adviser Faisal Shakar. The visit began in Fiji on July 31st, where they met with government officials, including Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka, and visited the Black Rock Camp. Mr. LeCroy commended Fiji for its longstanding commitment to UN peacekeeping. The delegation then traveled to Australia, where on August 2nd, Mr. LeCroy inaugurated the second UN Police Training Course in Brisbane, organized by the Australian Federal Police. The course brings together police officers from 11 Pacific nations and Timor-Leste, to prepare them for future deployments. The visit coincided with Australia marking 60 years since its first peacekeeping deployment, which was to Cyprus. In Canberra, he met with senior Australian defense and foreign affairs officials, including the Secretary of Defense and Chief of Defense Force, Admiral Mark Hammond. The delegation visited the Australian War Memorial to pay tribute to Australia's fallen peacekeepers and engaged with academia and civil society at the Australian National University. The trip concluded in Sydney where Mr. Lacroix joined a roundtable with civil society, public servants and academics at the Lowy Institute. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization today said the benchmark measure of world food commodity prices edged up in July as recent heatwaves and energy price dynamics pushed up quotations for cereals, vegetable oils and sugar. The FAO food price index averaged 131.1 points in July 2026, up 0.6% from its June level and 1% higher than its year earlier level. Global wheat prices, for instance, surged by 5.8% amid heightened concerns over continued disruptions to Black Sea export flows and the likely impact of recent heat waves on crop yields in several key producing countries. In July, the FAO sugar price index increased by 5.6 percent, due mainly to concerns about the potential impacts of persistent hot and dry weather on crop yields in the European Union and of El Nino-related weather conditions on production prospects in key producing countries in Asia. You can find the full report on the FAO website. Sunday is the International Day of the World's Indigenous Peoples.
